newsitem.title: USA: Fed wary on inflation, but doesn't look set to act.
newsitem.headline: Fed wary on inflation, but doesn't look set to act.

text.p: Federal Reserve policy-makers are wary about the risk of higher inflation but do not look ready to do anything about it yet.

"If the Fed believes that inflation is a serious risk, then it should, in the interests of sustaining economic growth, tighten," central bank Vice Chair Alice Rivlin said in an interview with Reuters. "It's just at the moment that's not crystal clear." Wall Street analysts generally expect the Fed to decide to hold rates steady at its next policy-making meeting July 1-2. Comments by Rivlin and other Fed officials buttress that view, although the policy-makers seem a bit more worried about the threat of higher inflation than the financial markets are.
In the interview with Reuters on Monday, Rivlin said the Fed faces a dilemma -- the economy is slowing from its rapid first-quarter pace but still faces a risk of higher inflation.
That dilemma, though, is not new and could confront the Fed for some time yet, she said. "It could be that way for months. This could be a very boring story," Rivlin said.

The inflation risk mainly stems from what Rivlin and other Fed officials describe as "very tight" labour markets. The unemployment rate, at a near-24-year low of 4.8 percent, stands at a level that in the past led to stepped-up wage demands and higher inflation. But, so far at least, that has not happened.
"We have inflation risk without inflation," Rivlin said.
The Labour Department reported Tuesday that consumer prices rose 0.1 percent in May from a month earlier. On a year-on-year basis, prices were up 2.2 percent in May.

Fed officials, though, worry that inflation has been held down by temporary factors that will eventually disappear. By some estimates, the strong dollar and the muted rise in health care and other employee benefits shaved a quarter to a half a percentage point off the inflation rate last year. "Dollar strength cannot be counted on indefinitely" to hold down import prices, Richmond Fed President Alfred Broaddus said earlier this month.

Fed officials also point out that U.S. job markets would be even tighter if not for a surprise surge in the labour force last year -- a surge that is unlikely to continue. "It's probably topped out," Rivlin said.
Despite those concerns, the inflation-wary central bank seems in no rush to raise interest rates further, especially at a time when economic growth is slowing.

The central bank was taken aback by the amount of criticism it received after it nudged rates up by a quarter percentage point in March. "I was a little bit surprised given the fact that the economy is doing so well," Rivlin said.
After soaring at a 5.8 percent annual clip in the first quarter -- its fastest pace in nine years -- the economy is expected to grow by 1 percent to 2 percent in the current quarter.
Some Fed officials suggested, though, that the slowdown was likely to prove temporary.
Rivlin described the economy as "very healthy. Although retail sales have ebbed recently, consumer confidence is strong, personal incomes are rising and employment is high," she said.
"It looks like a very strong economy," Rivlin said. "The main risk is inflation."
That suggests that the Fed may hold off from raising rates again until the fall, when growth picks up after its second-quarter lapse.
